content:
Earlier this year, I swapped a battery-powered push mower for a robot mower controllable via iPhone. That model lets you manually steer it around the perimeter of your yard to build a virtual map. Once set up, it automatically handles mowing on a schedule.

Recently, I tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a very different approach to navigation, and after several weeks of testing, I think it may be the easier choice for many people.

Camera-Based Automatic Mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each machine makes sense of your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK reference station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my iPhone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, by contrast, uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. Through three cameras, the mower can automatically map your lawn and navigate without the need for buried boundary wire or an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic method of creating the initial map did take longer, but for those who are less technically inclined, I think it may be easier to get started with.

To put that claim to the test, I had my mum, who lives in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She said everything worked fine. But I'm not entirely sure she would have had the patience to first manually drive a robot around the entire boundary, and then manually mark off the areas to avoid.

Automatic mapping produced a small quirk in my front yard. There's no fence or any physical separation between my lawn and my neighbour's, so TerraMow initially included part of the neighbour's grass in my map.

I sorted this out by marking that section as a no-go zone in the app. That said, if your lawn lacks a clear visual boundary, the initial mapping process may require a bit more attention.

A Look Through the Mower's Cameras

TerraMow's cameras also support one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to keep this view open in a large window. I could work indoors while watching, from the mower's perspective, as it moved around the back garden.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot far more engaging, and it occasionally helps explain why it slowed down or avoided something. The Anthbot M9 doesn't offer a similar camera view.

The two iPhone apps share quite a few concepts overall. Both let you schedule jobs, adjust mowing behaviour, divide zones, mark no-go areas, and take manual control of the mower.

When it comes to manually controlling the mower, TerraMow has one particularly standout design. In addition to the conventional left-and-right virtual joysticks, its app offers a single-handed operation mode. You can hold your iPhone in a natural posture and use your thumb to guide the mower.

Manually mowing with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot runs automatically on a schedule without any intervention. Still, TerraMow's joysticks are genuinely very handy when tidying up patches it missed.

At times, I felt almost as if I was controlling the machine with the Force (and it felt great). I could hold the iPhone down at my side, barely moving my thumb, and the mower would obediently follow my directions.

Every robot mower app should take a leaf out of this control design.

More Aggressive Mowing Performance

The TerraMow V1000 also gives off a more aggressive feel than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut closer to the ground and was noticeably louder while working.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow 'noisy'. However, the difference between the two is clear. The Anthbot can run so quietly that you almost forget it's still going, including when it mows after dark using its headlight.

Because TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. Daytime scheduling therefore becomes all the more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and robust, and is larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow bundles a protective garage that covers the charging dock, whereas Anthbot's garage is sold separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow performed consistently and reliably. I relied on it to handle the mowing for several weeks in a row without having to do it myself.

When Smart Maps Get Too Clever

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can occasionally work against it.

The mower continuously adjusts its map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes a while, during which you temporarily can't carry out other actions in the app.

I also ran into an interesting edge case. After several days of rain, parts of the yard had standing water, and TerraMow sensibly avoided that area during its next run.

The grass inside the skipped circular patch then grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to treat that growth as something to keep avoiding, and even after the ground dried, that patch of grass remained untouched.

I ended up using the app's remote-control function to manually steer the mower over the taller grass. Once that patch returned to its normal appearance, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regular edging also helps TerraMow approach boundaries with more confidence. If the grass is too long where the boundary is fuzzy, the mower may treat it as an obstacle rather than as part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive and more reliant on boundaries and obstacles you set yourself. That method requires more work up front, but it also avoids the map changing its mind about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac Verdict

Having used both systems, for most people I'd lean towards TerraMow's camera-based approach.

Burying boundary wire is simply not an option for me, and installing an RTK reference station means yet another piece of hardware to position, power, and maintain. TerraMow needs neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. The initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property line needed a manual fix, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook taller grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, a fascinating live camera view, and the best manual control experience I've come across in a robot mower app.

I actually enjoy looking after the yard, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. Handing that bit over to a robot frees up my time for landscaping, edging, and the finer details, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 does this well enough that I can recommend it, particularly for anyone who wants a robot mower but doesn't want to lay boundary wire, install an RTK antenna, or manually walk an iPhone around the entire yard.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently on sale on Amazon for US$999, after applying a US$200 coupon on the site. You can also buy it from TerraMow's official website.
